body.statement:
In the canonical full-observable experiment, suppose \(e_1\ne e_0\), \(p=1/2\), and \(\alpha+\beta<1\).  For every fixed \(a\) satisfying \(0<a\le2B\) and every integer \(n>4r+1\),
\[
 \frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}
 \le s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 \le \rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
Consequently, for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\) with \(\alpha+\beta<1\) and \(p=1/2\),
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The upper bound is witnessed by the unchanged sample-mean-centered test \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), viewed as a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The lower bound ranges over every common Borel randomized test of the vector containing the observed graph, assignments, exposures, realized outcomes, and known propensity coordinates.
body.proof_tex:
We first prove the upper bound.  Exposure positivity makes every score coordinate a Borel function of one realized outcome, its exposure indicators, and its two known propensity coordinates.  Hence the definition of the canonical full observation supplies a law-independent Borel map \(T_n\) with
\[
 W_n=T_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}). \tag{1}
\]
It follows that \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\), and therefore \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), is a common Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The size-and-separation theorem gives
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\phi_{n,\alpha}]le\alpha
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[1-\phi_{n,\alpha}]le\beta
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta), \tag{2}
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  The defining optimization over \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) therefore implies
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{3}
\]

For the converse, fix \(a\in(0,2B]\) and put \(b=a/2\), so \(0<b\le B\).  We construct a submodel inside the corrected class.  Take the deterministic nearest-neighbor line graph, iid \(U_i\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\), and conditionally independent waves with iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) coordinates.  Because \(e_1\ne e_0\), define
\[
 E_i(d,G)=
 \begin{cases}
 e_1,&d_i=1,\\
 e_0,&d_i=0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 C_i(d)=(d_i,d_{i+1})\in\mathcal C:=\{00,01,10,11\}. \tag{4}
\]
For \(v=(v_{00},v_{01},v_{10},v_{11})\in\{-b,b\}^4\), let
\[
 \mathcal H_0
 =\{v:v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}=0\}.
\]
This set has six elements.  Let \(Q_0\) be uniform on \(\mathcal H_0\), let
\[
 v^+=(-b,-b,b,b),
 \qquad v^-=-v^+,
\]
let \(Q_1=(\delta_{v^+}+\delta_{v^-})/2\), and define
\[
 Q_t=(1-t)Q_0+tQ_1,
 \qquad 0\le t<1. \tag{5}
\]
Enumerate the finite support of \(Q_t\), partition \([0,1]\) into consecutive half-open intervals having the corresponding \(Q_t\)-masses, and let \(F_t:[0,1]\to\{-b,b\}^4\) take the associated support value on each interval.  Then \(F_t\) is Borel and pushes the uniform law forward to \(Q_t\).  Put \(V_i=F_t(U_i)\), and use the same no-carryover schedule in both waves:
\[
 Y_i(d;U,G)=V_{i,C_i(d)}. \tag{6}
\]

We verify membership rather than treating (5)--(6) as if they implied it by definition.  The line graph is shift equivariant and has edge range one, which is at most \(r\) because \(r\) is a positive integer.  Equations (4) and (6) give
\[
 E_{i+k}(d,G)=E_i(\theta^kd,\theta^kG),
 \qquad
 Y_{i+k}(d;U,G)=Y_i(\theta^kd;\theta^kU,\theta^kG). \tag{7}
\]
More strongly, with no exceptional event at all, the single Borel map
\[
 \Psi_t((u_s)_{s=-r}^{r},(x_s)_{s=-r}^{r})
 =\begin{cases}
   \bigl(e_1,[F_t(u_0)]_{(x_0,x_1)}\bigr),&x_0=1,\\
   \bigl(e_0,[F_t(u_0)]_{(x_0,x_1)}\bigr),&x_0=0
  \end{cases} \tag{8}
\]
represents the exposure--outcome pair at every site after translating the local coordinates.  Thus (8) verifies the corrected joint assignment--innovation cylinder condition simultaneously for every assignment.  Also \(|Y_i|=b\le B\), and
\[
 \pi_i(e_1)=\pi_i(e_0)=\frac12>\varepsilon. \tag{9}
\]
Together with the iid innovations and the two Bernoulli waves, (7)--(9) verify every condition of \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Denote the resulting law by \(P_t\).

Given \(V_i=v\), averaging over the four equiprobable cells in (4) and using the exposure-IPW definition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 m_i
 &=\mathbb E_{P_t}\!\left[
 Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)
 \left\{
  \frac{\mathbf 1\{D_i^{(w)}=1\}}{1/2}
  -\frac{\mathbf 1\{D_i^{(w)}=0\}}{1/2}
 \right\}
 \middle|\mathcal F_U\right]\\
 &=\frac{v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}}2.
\end{aligned}\tag{10}
\]
Thus \(m_i=0\) under every schedule in \(\mathcal H_0\), whereas it equals \(a\) at \(v^+\) and \(-a\) at \(v^-\).  Symmetry gives \(\tau_{\mathrm P}=0\).  Because the schedules are iid over sites, \((h_i)=(m_i)\) is iid, and therefore
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=a^2t,
 \qquad \gamma_h(k)=0\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_t)=a^2t. \tag{11}
\]
In particular, \(P_0\) is a null law.  Equation (10) proves that (11) changes the conditional causal exposure-effect score, rather than defining the target through an observed-law functional.

We now bound the information in the complete declared observation.  Conditional on both assignment arrays, site \(i\) reveals the ordered coordinate pair \((V_{i,c},V_{i,c'})\), where \(c=C_i(D^{(1)})\) and \(c'=C_i(D^{(2)})\).  Let \(R_j^{c,c'}\) be its law under \(Q_j\), for \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and order the atoms as \((b,b),(b,-b),(-b,b),(-b,-b)\).  Exhaustive enumeration of all six elements of \(\mathcal H_0\) and the two elements \(v^+,v^-\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{ordered cell pair}&R_0^{c,c'}&R_1^{c,c'}\\ \hline
c=c'&(1/2,0,0,1/2)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\ne c'\text{ within one exposure group}
 &(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c,c'\text{ in opposite exposure groups}
 &(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)&(0,1/2,1/2,0).
\end{array} \tag{12}
\]
These rows cover all sixteen ordered pairs in \(\mathcal C^2\), providing the exact finite-cell stress test.  In every row, every atom charged by \(R_1^{c,c'}\) has positive \(R_0^{c,c'}\)-probability.  Hence the induced two-wave observed-outcome laws have common support even though the latent four-cell schedule laws need not.

Let \(R_t^{c,c'}=(1-t)R_0^{c,c'}+tR_1^{c,c'}\).  Direct substitution in (12) yields
\[
 \sum_x\frac{\{R_1^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}
 {R_0^{c,c'}(x)}
 =\begin{cases}0,&c=c',\\2,&c\ne c'.\end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
For probability masses \(R\ll S\), the elementary inequality \(\log u\le u-1\) gives
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(R\Vert S)
 \le\sum_x\frac{(R(x)-S(x))^2}{S(x)}. \tag{14}
\]
Applying (14) with (13) proves
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{c,c'}\Vert R_0^{c,c'})\le2t^2. \tag{15}
\]

Conditional on the full assignments, the selected outcome pairs are independent over \(i\in I_n\), since each pair uses only \(V_i\).  The graph and assignment laws coincide under \(P_t\) and \(P_0\), while exposures and propensity coordinates are deterministic functions of them.  Conditional on the assignments, the Radon--Nikodym derivative of the outcome law is the product of the \(N_n\) sitewise derivatives.  Taking its logarithm, then its conditional expectation, turns that product into the following sum; averaging over the common assignment law and using (15) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\operatorname{KL}\!\left(
  \mathcal L_{P_t}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
  \middle\Vert
  \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \right)\\
 &\quad=\mathbb E_D\sum_{i\in I_n}
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(
  R_t^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}
  \middle\Vert
  R_0^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}
 \right)
 \le2N_nt^2.
\end{aligned}\tag{16}
\]
Thus (16) controls the complete declared record, not merely the score vector.

Put \(\eta=1-\alpha-\beta>0\) and
\[
 t_0=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2N_n}}.
\]
Since \(0<\eta<1\) and \(N_n\ge1\), \(0<t_0<1\), so \(P_{t_0}\) belongs to the submodel.  The cited Pinsker lemma and (16) imply
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(
  \mathcal L_{P_{t_0}}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}),
  \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \right)
 \le\sqrt{N_nt_0^2}=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}. \tag{17}
\]
Let \(\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) have type-I error at most \(\alpha\) under every null law.  To cover randomized tests by the cited binary Le Cam lemma, adjoin under both laws the same independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and reject exactly when \(A\le\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  If \(\mu,\nu\) are the two laws of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) and \(\lambda\) is the uniform law, then for every measurable \(H\), sectioning and integration give
\[
 |(\mu\times\lambda)(H)-(\nu\times\lambda)(H)|
 \le\int |\mu(H_u)-\nu(H_u)|\,d\lambda(u)
 \le\operatorname{TV}(\mu,\nu).
\]
The reverse inequality follows by taking \(H=C\times[0,1]\) and then the supremum over measurable \(C\).  Hence product with the common uniform law preserves total variation.  The Le Cam lemma and (17) yield
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{t_0}}[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}
 =\beta+\eta\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
 >\beta. \tag{18}
\]
By (11),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_{t_0})
 =\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{19}
\]
For every proposed separation no larger than (19), the alternative set contains \(P_{t_0}\), while (18) rules out the required type-II guarantee for every test meeting the uniform null guarantee.  Taking the infimum in the definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) proves
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 \ge\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{20}
\]
Combining (3) and (20), fixing any \(a\in(0,2B]\), using \(N_n=n-2r\), and using the proved bound \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\), establishes \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2})\).  Distinct labels are necessary for this witness: if \(e_1=e_0\), the two terms in every exposure-IPW score cancel identically.
body.justification: A causal-realizable four-cell schedule verifies corrected class membership and gives a common-support likelihood bound for every Borel test of the complete declared record.
body.gap: Viviano2020 optimizes a second-wave design after a pilot; it does not prove a full-observation information lower bound for testing the Palm covariance boundary.
body.consumer: A designer can use the finite-sample upper threshold knowing that no common Borel test of the declared full observation improves its separation order uniformly over the class.
